canonical_statement: The study was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, single-center clinical trial conducted at the University of Minnesota during the 2023–2024 and 2024–2025 influenza seasons.
The study used three in-person visits: baseline, 4–6 weeks after baseline, and 16–18 weeks after baseline.
Blood samples were obtained at all three study visits.
At visit 2, randomization was performed 1:1 by the investigational pharmacy using permuted blocks.
Participants, clinical staff, and research personnel remained blinded to second-injection assignment until study completion.
At the end of the influenza season, investigators reviewed medical records and queried participants about influenza-like illness and laboratory-confirmed respiratory infections.
Adverse events were graded using the 2007 FDA preventive-vaccine toxicity grading scale from grade 1 through grade 5.
The primary outcome was immunogenicity measured as fold change in geometric mean titers of ID80 neutralizing and binding antibodies to influenza vaccine strains from baseline to the 4-month visit.

outcome.definition: Fold change in GMTs of ID80 neutralizing and binding antibodies from baseline to 4 months
outcome.measurement_method: ID80 neutralization assay and binding antibody assay

canonical_statement: Secondary clinical outcomes were influenza-related pneumonia, hospitalization, ICU admission, and death during the influenza season.

outcome.definition: Pneumonia, hospitalization, ICU admission, or death during the influenza season

canonical_statement: Safety outcomes were adverse events including solicited local and systemic reactogenicity.

outcome.definition: Clinical AEs including solicited local and systemic reactogenicity

canonical_statement: Neutralizing antibody responses were measured with replication-restricted influenza reporter viruses; ID50 and ID80 were interpolated from five-parameter logistic regression curves.
Binding antibody responses were measured by electrochemiluminescence immunoassay and reported as arbitrary units per milliliter.
The planned sample size was 47 participants per arm to provide 80% power to detect a geometric mean ratio of 3.0 at a two-sided alpha of 0.05.
Primary analyses used the intention-to-treat population.
Phuket-strain analyses were restricted to participants enrolled in the 2023–2024 season because Phuket was not included in the 2024–2025 vaccine formulation.
For each strain and assay, geometric mean fold rise was the geometric mean of the individual fold changes from baseline to the 4-month visit.

Between-group geometric mean ratios were estimated with generalized estimating equations on log-transformed titers using a Gaussian identity-link model, exchangeable working correlation, and robust variance estimation.

The primary analysis used multiple imputation for missing 4-month titers with treatment arm, age, sex, prior-season influenza vaccination, transplant timing, maintenance immunosuppression, and baseline titer in the imputation model.
Prespecified exploratory analyses evaluated ID50 neutralizing titers and geometric mean fold rises from baseline to 1 month and from 1 month to 4 months.
Holm correction was applied across influenza strains to control the family-wise error rate for immunogenicity comparisons.
Of 228 people prescreened, 74 consented and enrolled.

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that an in-season second high-dose influenza vaccine dose may improve influenza-specific antibody responses compared with a single high-dose dose in adult solid organ transplant recipients.
The authors stated that confirmation in larger adequately powered studies is required before the booster strategy can be established.
The authors considered the safety profile of the two-dose high-dose regimen reassuring because adverse events were generally mild and not more frequent in the 2 HD group.
Enrollment did not reach the planned target sample size, reducing statistical power.
Several participants missed the 4-month visit, further reducing statistical power for primary and secondary analyses.
The exploratory post-randomization immunogenicity findings require cautious interpretation because they were not primary efficacy analyses.
The cohort was predominantly kidney and liver transplant recipients, limiting generalizability to other transplant types, including lung transplant recipients.
Participants less than 1 year after solid organ transplantation were excluded, so findings cannot be generalized to that early post-transplant population.
The study did not include a dedicated 4–6 week visit after the second injection and therefore could not directly assess peak post-booster antibody responses.
Influenza-like illness was ascertained at the end of the season without active surveillance and may have been underestimated.
The influenza assays did not include hemagglutination-inhibition titers for seroprotection and seroconversion correlates.
The Fluzone vaccine formulation differed between the two study seasons.
The assays used cell-based influenza strains with 98–100% amino-acid homology to the egg-based vaccine strains rather than perfectly matched vaccine strains.
The trial was not powered to determine clinical vaccine effectiveness, and only two laboratory-confirmed influenza events occurred.
Study data are available from the investigators upon reasonable request.
The authors reported no competing interests.

The study was supported by internal University of Minnesota funding and in part by the NIH Intramural Research Program; the authors stated that funders had no role in study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, publication decision, or manuscript writing.
